members.summary: Frozen configuration for the I-JEPA family.
members.extended: Defaults are the paper's ViT-B/16 (Table 1, Appendix A.1).

parameters.name: image_size
parameters.description: Input resolution.  The 448-pixel variant is the one exception.

parameters.name: patch_size
parameters.description: Patch side; `image_size` must be a multiple of it.

parameters.name: in_channels
parameters.description: Image channels.

parameters.name: num_classes
parameters.description: Classes the linear probe predicts.  Pretraining ignores it.

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: The encoder, which is a ViT of the named size.

parameters.name: depth
parameters.description: The encoder, which is a ViT of the named size.

parameters.name: num_heads
parameters.description: The encoder, which is a ViT of the named size.

parameters.name: mlp_ratio
parameters.description:
Feed-forward width as a multiple of `dim`.  ViT-g/16 is the one
variant where the paper uses a different ratio.

parameters.name: layer_norm_eps
parameters.description: Epsilon of every LayerNorm.

parameters.name: predictor_dim
parameters.description:
Predictor width, for every variant (Appendix A.1; Table 14 measures
384 against 1024 and prefers it).  The predictor is deliberately
narrower than the encoder.

parameters.name: predictor_depth
parameters.description: Predictor blocks: 6 for ViT-B/16, 12 for the larger encoders.

parameters.name: predictor_heads
parameters.description:
Heads inside the predictor.  `None` takes the encoder's count,
which is what the released code does — so a 16-head predictor 384
wide has 24-dimensional heads.

parameters.name: num_target_blocks
parameters.description:
Target blocks predicted per image (Section 3).  They may overlap
each other.

parameters.name: target_scale
parameters.description: Fraction of the image each target block covers.

parameters.name: target_aspect
parameters.description: Aspect-ratio range of a target block.

parameters.name: context_scale
parameters.description:
Fraction of the image the context block covers.  Its aspect ratio
is 1 — *not stated* in the paper, fixed in the released code.

parameters.name: min_keep
parameters.description:
Patches a sampled block must exceed, or it is resampled.  *Not
stated*; the released configs set it.

parameters.name: allow_overlap
parameters.description:
Whether the context may keep patches that fall inside a target
block.  The paper removes them; the released code makes it a flag
and sets it False.

parameters.name: ema
parameters.description:
Momentum of the target encoder at the first and last training step,
moving linearly between them.

parameters.name: objective
parameters.description:
How predicted and target representations are compared.  ⚠️ The
paper states an $\ell_2$ loss; the released code — which
produced the released checkpoints — uses smooth L1.  The default
follows the code, and `"l2"` is the paper's.

parameters.name: smooth_l1_beta
parameters.description: Where smooth L1 turns from quadratic to linear.

examples:
>>> from lucid.models.vision.ijepa import IJEPAConfig
>>> config = IJEPAConfig()
>>> config.num_patches, config.grid_size
(196, 14)
>>> config.predictor_dim, config.num_target_blocks
(384, 4)
The predictor takes the encoder's head count when it is not given:
>>> IJEPAConfig(num_heads=16, predictor_heads=None).resolved_predictor_heads
16
notes:
Reference: Assran, Mahmoud, et al., *"Self-Supervised Learning from
Images with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture"*, CVPR 2023
([arXiv:2301.08243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08243)), Table 1 for the variants and Appendix A.1 for the
masking and the momentum schedule.

members.summary: A linear probe on I-JEPA's representation.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Frozen configuration; `num_classes` sizes the head.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.ijepa import (
...     IJEPAConfig, IJEPAForImageClassification)
>>> config = IJEPAConfig(
...     image_size=32, patch_size=8, dim=16, depth=1, num_heads=2,
...     predictor_dim=8, predictor_depth=1, num_classes=10, min_keep=1)
>>> model = IJEPAForImageClassification(config).eval()
>>> model(lucid.rand(2, 3, 32, 32)).logits.shape
(2, 10)
notes:
Reference: Assran et al., [arXiv:2301.08243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08243), Appendix A.2 — the paper
evaluates by linear probing the frozen target encoder, which is what
this is.  The target encoder cannot be trained through this class: its
parameters are frozen where they are built, so an optimiser handed
everything still only moves the head.

It carries the whole pretraining model — both encoders and the
predictor — because that is what a checkpoint holds and what
continuing to pretrain would need.  Inference uses one of the three,
so an exported package is about three times the size it has to be.

Linear between `config.ema[0]` and `config.ema[1]` — 0.996

methods.name: update_target
methods.summary: Move the target encoder toward the context encoder.
methods.extended:
Call it after the optimiser step: this writes parameters in place,
and doing that while a graph that read them is alive would sever
the two.

parameters.name: momentum
parameters.description: Weight kept on the target encoder, from `momentum`.

methods.name: encode
methods.extended:
Appendix A.1 evaluates the *target* encoder, average-pooled over
patches — not the context encoder, which is a silent accuracy loss.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: Images `(B, C, H, W)`.

notes:
Not wrapped in `no_grad`: the target encoder's parameters are
frozen already, so nothing accumulates into them, and a method a
probe reads through should not sever the gradient a probe needs.
The stop-gradient that matters is in `forward`, where the
targets are built.

members.summary: I-JEPA: a context encoder, an averaged target encoder, a predictor.

parameters.name: config
parameters.description: Frozen configuration.

examples:
>>> import lucid
>>> from lucid.models.vision.ijepa import IJEPAConfig, IJEPAModel
>>> config = IJEPAConfig(
...     image_size=32, patch_size=8, dim=16, depth=1, num_heads=2,
...     predictor_dim=8, predictor_depth=1, min_keep=1,
...     target_scale=(0.1, 0.2), context_scale=(0.8, 1.0))
>>> model = IJEPAModel(config)
>>> out = model(lucid.rand(2, 3, 32, 32))
>>> out.prediction.shape == out.target.shape
True
>>> float(out.loss.item()) >= 0.0
True
The representation a downstream task uses is the target encoder's,
average-pooled:
>>> model.encode(lucid.rand(2, 3, 32, 32)).shape
(2, 16)
notes:
Reference: Assran, Mahmoud, et al., *"Self-Supervised Learning from
Images with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture"*, CVPR 2023
([arXiv:2301.08243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08243)), Section 3 and Appendix A.1.

The target encoder is not updated by the optimiser.  Call
`update_target` after each step, with
`momentum` for the value the schedule asks for.

Two details come from the released code rather than the paper: the
target representations are layer-normalised (without affine terms)
before the loss reads them, and that loss is smooth L1 where the paper
writes $\ell_2$.  `config.objective` selects between them.

attributes.name: encoder
attributes.description: The context encoder — the one that is trained.

attributes.name: target_encoder
attributes.description:
Its exponential moving average.  Frozen; produces the targets and,
after pretraining, the representation everything downstream uses.

attributes.name: predictor
attributes.description: The narrow transformer that answers for blocks it was not given.

summary: I-JEPA — self-supervised pretraining that predicts representations.
extended:
Assran et al., CVPR 2023 ([arXiv:2301.08243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08243)).  A context block is encoded,
and a narrow predictor must say what an exponential moving average of that
encoder would report about four blocks it was never shown.  Nothing is
reconstructed in pixel space, which is the point.
citation: Assran, Mahmoud, et al. "Self-Supervised Learning from Images with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2023.
theory:
I-JEPA asks a question about an image and grades the answer in
representation space.  One *context* block is encoded by
$f_\theta$; four *target* blocks are encoded by a second network
$f_{\bar\theta}$, and a predictor $g_\phi$ must produce the
target encoder's output for each target block from the context alone,
told only *where* each block is:



$$
\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{i=1}^{M} \sum_{j \in B_i}
d\bigl(\hat s_{y_j},\, s_{y_j}\bigr), \qquad
\hat s_{y} = g_\phi\bigl(f_\theta(x_{\text{context}}),\, p_y\bigr).
$$

**The target is a representation, not a pixel.**  A generative
objective must account for every detail that distinguishes one plausible
completion from another --- the exact texture of grass, the grain of a
wall --- and spends capacity doing so.  Predicting $f_{\bar\theta}$'s
output lets the model drop whatever that encoder has already learned to
drop.  The paper's ablation is unusually clean: the same architecture
trained against pixels reaches 40.7% on 1% of ImageNet, and against
representations 66.9%.

**The target encoder is the model's own past.**  $f_{\bar\theta}$
is not trained; its weights are an exponential moving average of
$f_\theta$, with the momentum moving linearly from 0.996 to 1 over
training.  There is no gradient path into it at all, which is what stops
the pair from agreeing on a constant --- the target moves only as fast
as the average lets it.

**The masking carries the difficulty.**  Four target blocks covering
15--20% of the image each, at aspect ratios from 3:4 to 3:2, with a
context block of 85--100% from which every target region is then
removed.  Predicting a large connected region from a large connected
region is what forces semantics; the paper's ablation against
rasterised or small random masks (54.2% versus 15.5% and 17.6%) is a
statement about the task, not the architecture.

**No** $[\text{cls}]$ **token.**  Evaluation average-pools the
target encoder's patch outputs.
